Background structure

Words: 45
Mathematical physics OurBigBook.com
Geometric or field data held fixed when a theory's dynamical degrees of freedom vary. The Minkowski metric is background structure in ordinary special relativity; the spacetime metric tensor is dynamical in general relativity. A fixed timelike vector field can introduce a preferred direction even when an equation is written using tensor notation.

Time scale (τ)

Words: 41
Mathematical physics OurBigBook.com
A time scale is a characteristic duration over which a specified variable or process changes appreciably. Comparing time scales helps choose a dimensionless time and identify a singular perturbation. An exponential relaxation x−x∗​=Ae−t/τ has relaxation time constant τ; a nonlinear process can have several distinct time scales.

Compactification (physics)

Words: 2k Articles: 29
Mathematical physics OurBigBook.com
Compactification makes some spatial dimensions compact, so modes along them acquire discrete momenta. At energies below the first nonzero compact-mode mass, a dimensional reduction to the zero modes gives a lower-dimensional effective field theory. The compact volume fixes the gravitational kinetic coefficient in an unwarped product background.

Brane-world scenario

Words: 61
Compactification (physics) OurBigBook.com
In a brane-world model some fields, typically ordinary matter and gauge fields, are localized on a lower-dimensional brane, while gravity propagates through the higher-dimensional bulk. Compact volume or a warped metric can then separate the observed gravitational scale from local matter scales. A model must specify field localization, boundary conditions and stabilization rather than identifying a brane with an arbitrary compactification.

Kaluza-Klein theory (ds2=gμν​dxμdxν+R2(dy+Aμ​dxμ)2)

Words: 413 Articles: 5
Compactification (physics) OurBigBook.com
Kaluza-Klein theory obtains lower-dimensional fields from a higher-dimensional metric and other fields on compact dimensions. In the displayed fixed-radius circle ansatz, the off-diagonal metric supplies a vector. The coordinate change y↦y+λ(x) is compensated by A↦A−dλ, producing an Abelian gauge symmetry. Allowing the radius to vary adds a scalar modulus. Kaluza-Klein modes also include nonzero internal momenta, giving a tower of massive fields.

Periodic electrostatic Green function with one compact dimension (ϕ(r,z)=2πrq​cosh(r/R)−cos(z/R)sinh(r/R)​)

Words: 76
Kaluza-Klein theory OurBigBook.com
For the Poisson equation ∇42​ϕ=−4πRqδ3(x)δ2πR​(z) on R3×S1, expand the periodic delta as (2πR)−1∑n​einz/R. The nth Kaluza-Klein mode has radial potential qe−∣n∣r/R/(2πr), since (∇32​−m2)e−mr/r=−4πδ3(x). Summing the geometric series gives the displayed Green function. At equal compact coordinate it reduces to qcoth(r/(2R))/(2πr). Thus the interaction energy changes from q1​q2​/(2πr) at large separation to q1​q2​R/(πr2) at small separation, with normalization fixed by the stated Poisson equation.

Retarded circle-compactified massless propagator (Gret​=R−1∑n​e2πinΔw/RGret(4,mn​)​,mn​=2π∣n∣/R)

Words: 120 Articles: 1
Kaluza-Klein theory OurBigBook.com
For a massless field on Minkowski space times a circle of circumference R, the compact delta distribution expands as R−1∑n​e2πinΔw/R. The noncompact retarded Green function in each Fourier sector is that of a four-dimensional field with mass mn​. Equivalently, the time-frequency denominator is k2+mn2​−(ω+i0)2, putting both poles below the real axis. At equal compact positions the sum has one zero mode and a doubly counted nonzero mass tower.
Static Green function across a circle compactification (Gstat​(r,0)=[4πRr]−1coth(πr/R))
Words: 48
Retarded circle-compactified massless propagator OurBigBook.com
At zero frequency, sum the Kaluza-Klein tower of three-spatial-dimensional Yukawa kernels: [4πRr]−1(1+2∑n≥1​e−2πnr/R). The geometric series gives the displayed function. It behaves as 1/(4π2r2) for r≪R, the four-spatial-dimensional Coulomb kernel, and as 1/(4πRr) for r≫R, the three-spatial-dimensional kernel with a zero-mode normalization factor.

Maxwell reduction on a circle (mn​=∣n∣/r)

Words: 98
Kaluza-Klein theory OurBigBook.com
A real five-dimensional Maxwell field on a circle of radius r has a Fourier series with coefficients AM(n)​, AM(−n)​=(AM(n)​)∗. Its mixed field-strength component is Fμ5(n)​=∂μ​A5(n)​−inAμ(n)​/r. The nonzero modes transform as δAμ(n)​=∂μ​Λ(n), δA5(n)​=inΛ(n)/r. Thus A5(n)​ is a Stueckelberg mechanism field and the gauge-invariant massive vector is Aμ(n)​−r∂μ​A5(n)​/(in). Its mass is ∣n∣/r and it has three physical polarizations. The zero modes instead consist of a massless four-dimensional Maxwell field and a real massless scalar field; the latter cannot be removed by a periodic infinitesimal gauge transformation. A positive Fourier level and its negative level are conjugate, not independent real fields.

Kaluza-Klein monopole

Words: 54
Kaluza-Klein theory OurBigBook.com
A gravitational magnetic monopole for a compact circle, whose fibre is nontrivially twisted over a surrounding two-sphere. With flat spectator directions its nonsingular local geometry is a Taub–NUT space. Reducing along the M-circle yields the D6-brane. The magnetic dual of the IIB circle vector is instead a five-brane in nine noncompact dimensions.

Radion

Words: 194 Articles: 2
Compactification (physics) OurBigBook.com
A radion is a lower-dimensional scalar field describing the size or separation modulus of compact extra dimensions. In a two-brane Randall–Sundrum model, its expectation determines the inter-brane separation and the warp-generated hierarchy. A background size alone does not supply a radion potential or a stabilization mechanism.
// Target: supersymmetry.bigb

Radius stabilization (V′(R0​)=0,mR2​>0)

Words: 148 Articles: 1
Radion OurBigBook.com
Radius stabilization fixes the size of a compactification dynamically rather than choosing it as an undetermined parameter. If the four-dimensional low-energy effective action contains a radion R with positive kinetic coefficient Z(R) and scalar potential V(R), a stable radius R0​ requires V′(R0​)=0 and mR2​=V′′(R0​)/Z(R0​)>0. This matters for the hierarchy problem: the volume or warp factor explains a hierarchy only if a consistent dynamics selects and maintains the required geometry.
Goldberger–Wise stabilization mechanism (kL≃ϵ−1log(v0​/vL​))
Words: 87
Radius stabilization OurBigBook.com
The Goldberger–Wise stabilization mechanism generates a radion potential in the Randall–Sundrum model using a weakly backreacting bulk scalar field. On 0≤y≤L, its static profile obeys χ′′−4kχ′−mχ2​χ=0, hence χ=Ae(4+ϵ)ky+Be−ϵky, where ϵ=4+mχ2​/k2​−2. Boundary potentials approximately fix χ(0)=v0​, χ(L)=vL​. For ϵ≪1 and kL≫1, the leading radius-dependent potential is proportional to e−4kL(vL​−v0​e−ϵkL)2. Its leading minimum satisfies kL≃ϵ−1log(v0​/vL​). Thus a modest ratio of boundary values can generate a large warp exponent. Corrections shift this minimum; the approximation requires small scalar field backreaction, and the four-dimensional cosmological constant still needs adjustment.

Randall–Sundrum model (ds2=e−2k∣y∣ημν​dxμdxν+dy2)

Words: 307 Articles: 4
Compactification (physics) OurBigBook.com
A warped five-dimensional geometry redshifts masses of fields localized on the distant brane: mIR​=e−kLm0​. For the usual doubled orbifold interval, integration of the Einstein-Hilbert action gives MPl2​=M53​(1−e−2kL)/k. Exponential redshift can generate a large separation of observable scales with a moderately sized dimensionless distance kL. Stabilizing the radion remains a dynamical requirement.

High-energy braneworld expansion (H2=38πG​ρ(1+2λρ​)+a4C​)

Words: 119 Articles: 1
Randall–Sundrum model OurBigBook.com
For a spatially flat, tuned one-brane background without energy transfer to the bulk, the Israel junction conditions produce the displayed modified Friedmann equation. Positive brane tension λ gives ordinary expansion when ρ≪λ, while the quadratic density correction enhances expansion at high energy. Big Bang nucleosynthesis, early acoustic evolution and primordial spectra can constrain this change. Spatial curvature, a residual cosmological constant and bulk energy exchange require their additional terms rather than this special formula.
Dark radiation on a cosmological brane (ρE​∝Ca−4)
Words: 52
High-energy braneworld expansion OurBigBook.com
Projected bulk Weyl tensor can contribute a radiation-scaling term to the brane Friedmann equation, even without ordinary brane photons. For an anti-de Sitter black-hole bulk the integration constant is related to its mass. This dark radiation on a cosmological brane changes the expansion rate tested by Big Bang nucleosynthesis and Cosmic microwave background anisotropy; it should not automatically be identified with a freely specifiable thermal particle species.

Gravity localization in a noncompact warped dimension (M42​=M53​∫−∞∞​e−2k∣y∣dy=M53​/k)

Words: 132 Articles: 1

The harmonic oscillator equation gives F→2π at small amplitude; the full simple pendulum supplies its finite-amplitude correction. A model with drag or a finite massive support has additional parameters, so the same dimensional argument does not automatically apply.
The result is useful for comparison: at fixed angular amplitude and g, lengths in the ratio 1:4 give periods in the ratio 1:2. The ratio Tg/ℓ​ should be the same for both in this ideal model. Hydrogen atom OurBigBook.com
A family of hydrogen emission lines terminating at a fixed lower principal quantum number nf​. In the nonrelativistic Bohr model, their inverse wavelengths are 1/λ=RH​(1/nf2​−1/ni2​) for integers ni​>nf​. Holding nf​ fixed and increasing ni​ gives lines approaching the series limit 1/λ=RH​/nf2​. Reduced mass shifts the Rydberg constant, while additional interactions produce corrections to this gross spectral pattern.

Brackett series (n→4)

Words: 32
Hydrogen spectral series OurBigBook.com
The Brackett series consists of hydrogen spectral lines with final principal quantum number four and initial principal quantum number greater than four. The Rydberg formula gives 1/λ=RH​(1/16−1/n2). Its infrared wavelengths make these recombination lines less susceptible to interstellar extinction than optical Balmer series lines; quantitative use requires the appropriate effective recombination coefficient.

Rydberg constant (R∞​)

Words: 43
Rydberg formula OurBigBook.com
The inverse-length constant in the infinite-nuclear-mass hydrogenic spectrum, R∞​=me​e4/[8ϵ02​h3c]. A nucleus of finite mass replaces it by RM​=R∞​μ/me​, where μ is the electron-nucleus reduced mass. Some spectroscopic fits call Z2RM​ an effective Rydberg constant; the charge-inclusive and reduced-mass-only conventions must be distinguished.

The Lyman limit is the short-wavelength limit of transitions to the hydrogen atom ground state. Its photon energy, approximately 13.6eV, is the ground-state ionization energy.

Lyman-alpha line (λα​≃1216A˚)

Hydrogen atom OurBigBook.com
The Lyman-alpha line is the hydrogen 2p↔1s electric-dipole transition, with photon energy about 10.2eV and vacuum wavelength about 1216 angstroms. Its emission cools collisionally excited gas, while absorption traces neutral hydrogen along a background-source sightline.

Lyman-alpha absorption (1s+γ→2p)

Words: 507 Articles: 8
Lyman-alpha line OurBigBook.com
A neutral hydrogen atom absorbs a photon near the Lyman-alpha resonance by excitation from 1s to 2p. Absorption lines in a quasar spectrum can therefore locate hydrogen along the sightline by their redshift, subject to peculiar-velocity and line-profile effects.
Damped Lyman-alpha system (NHI​≳2×1020cm−2)
Words: 45
Lyman-alpha absorption OurBigBook.com
A damped Lyman-alpha system has a sufficiently high neutral-hydrogen column density that the Lorentzian wings of its Voigt profile are conspicuous. These wings come from the finite lifetime of the excited atomic state, not from unusually high gas temperature. Damped systems usually trace substantial neutral reservoirs associated with galaxies.
Lyman limit system (NHI​≳1017.2cm−2)

Lyman-alpha absorption OurBigBook.com
A Lyman limit system has approximately unit or greater optical depth at the neutral-hydrogen Lyman limit near 91.2nm. The threshold follows from τ912​=NHI​σ912​ with σ912​≃6.3×10−18cm2. Its strong continuum absorption distinguishes it from ordinary weak Lyman-alpha forest lines. Classification conventions often separate damped Lyman-alpha systems as the highest-column category.

Lyman-alpha absorption OurBigBook.com
The neutral-hydrogen column-density distribution counts Lyman-alpha absorption systems per unit column density and redshift. A count in logarithmic column bins is Nln(10)f(N,z). A distribution per absorption distance instead removes the geometrical path factor.

A circular, opaque, geometrically thin disk has projected area πR2∣cosi∣. For isotropically oriented normals, ∣cosi∣ is uniform on [0,1], so the mean interception area is half the face-on area. A nonunit covering fraction multiplies this cross-section. Lyman-alpha emission (2p→1s+γ)

Words: 45
Lyman-alpha line OurBigBook.com
Radiative decay from the hydrogen 2p level to 1s produces a Lyman-alpha photon. In an optically thin collisionally excited gas, escape of this photon removes the excitation energy deposited by an electron collision. The excitation threshold is responsible for the rapid temperature sensitivity of this cooling channel.

Bohr model

Words: 965 Articles: 3
Hydrogen atom OurBigBook.com
The Bohr model assumes circular electron orbits with quantized orbital angular momentum Nℏ. It reproduces the hydrogen energy levels, but wavefunctions in quantum mechanics describe spatial probability distributions rather than definite trajectories. In particular, spherically symmetric Coulomb bound states have zero orbital angular momentum.
The puzzle is the coexistence of reproducible spectral lines and stable chemical atoms. A classical circular orbit in a Coulomb potential can have any negative energy: Coulomb's law alone selects no special radius or emitted frequency. Moreover, its electron has centripetal acceleration. The Larmor formula then predicts positive radiated power, so conservation of energy makes the orbit shrink. Simply drawing concentric circles explains neither stability nor a discrete spectrum.
Niels Bohr postulated nonradiating stationary states and emission with hν=Ei​−Ef​. His circular-orbit condition is L=nℏ. These assumptions override classical radiation; the emitted frequency need not equal an orbital frequency.[ref]

Circular-orbit derivation of the Bohr model (rn​=n2ℏ2/(μκ),En​=−μκ2/(2ℏ2n2))

Words: 275
Bohr model OurBigBook.com
Consider a single electron of mass me​ and a point atomic nucleus of mass M and positive electric charge Ze, with e>0 the elementary charge. Use nonrelativistic classical mechanics, omit external fields and interactions with other electrons, and write
μ=me​+Mme​M​,κ=4πϵ0​Ze2​,ℏ=2πh​.
(14)
Here μ is the Coulomb two-body reduced mass, ϵ0​ the vacuum permittivity, and h the Planck constant. The separation r and relative speed v describe the two-particle relative coordinate; neither body is silently pinned in place. The electron's own radius about the centre of mass is Mr/(M+me​).
For the assumed circular orbit, Coulomb's law provides the required centripetal acceleration, and the imposed orbital angular momentum condition is
rμv2​=r2κ​,L=μvr=nℏ,n=1,2,3,….
(15)
Substitute v=nℏ/(μr) into the first equation and cancel r−2 to obtain
rn​=μκn2ℏ2​,vn​=nℏκ​.
(16)
The kinetic energy is K=μv2/2=κ/(2r) and the Coulomb potential energy is U=−κ/r, with zero energy at infinite separation. Hence
En​=K+U=−2rn​κ​=−2(4πϵ0​)2ℏ2n2μZ2e4​.
(17)
This derives the energy sequence from the stated circular model; the modern Schrödinger equation derivation is the distinct series-termination quantization of the Coulomb radial equation. The radius above scales as n2/Z, whereas the binding energy scales as μZ2/n2. The Bohr radius article supplies the corresponding Coulomb potential length scale. The nonrelativistic assumption requires vn​≪c, with c the speed of light.
For an original numerical example choose Z=1, M=1.67262192369×10−27kg, me​=9.1093837015×10−31kg, e=1.602176634×10−19C, h=6.62607015×10−34Js, ϵ0​=8.8541878128×10−12Fm−1, and c=299792458ms−1. Treat these as stipulated constants for the calculation. They give μ/me​=0.99945568, r1​=0.0529465nm, E1​=−13.598287eV and v1​/c≃0.00730, where eV denotes an electronvolt. At n=2, r2​=4r1​ and E2​=E1​/4; the ground-state ionization energy is −E1​.
Taking M→∞ gives μ→me​. A finite nuclear mass reduces every binding energy by μ/me​ and increases each separation by me​/μ. This follows from relative motion, not a fitted correction to individual spectral lines. Replacing the atomic nucleus by a heavier isotope changes the same factor, providing another check of the model.

Hydrogen transition wavelengths in the Bohr model (λ−1=RH​(nf−2​−ni−2​))

Bohr model OurBigBook.com
For emission take integers ni​>nf​≥1. Applying conservation of energy to the model's internal energy difference, while neglecting the much smaller whole-atom photon recoil, gives
ΔE=Eni​​−Enf​​=BH​(nf2​1​−ni2​1​),BH​=2(4πϵ0​)2ℏ2μe4​,
(18)
ν=hΔE​,λ=νc​,λ1​=RH​(nf2​1​−ni2​1​),RH​=hcBH​​.
(19)
Thus Johannes Robert Rydberg's Rydberg formula is a difference of two energy levels expressed as a spectroscopic wavenumber. The same constants determine every line; there is no new parameter for each electronic transition. With the chosen inputs, RH​=1.096775834×107m−1. All wavelengths below are calculated in vacuum, not air, and are rounded model predictions rather than historical measurements.

The conventional names commemorate Theodore Lyman and Johann Jakob Balmer. Fixing nf​=1 produces the ultraviolet Lyman series, beginning with the Lyman-alpha line; fixing nf​=2 produces the Balmer series. As ni​→∞, the wavelength approaches nf2​/RH​: 91.1763nm at the Lyman limit and 364.705nm for the Balmer series. Crowding follows directly from En+1​−En​∼2BH​/n3. Discreteness therefore coexists with a series limit.
Correct line positions do not give wave intensities, lifetimes or electric-dipole selection rules for hydrogen. Those require a theory of the wavefunctions and their coupling to electromagnetic radiation. The circular model also omits spin, relativistic corrections and the Lamb shift. Its successful gross energy levels do not make its assumed orbits modern atomic orbitals.

Discharge spectra and the Bohr model

Words: 328
Bohr model OurBigBook.com
In On the Constitution of Atoms and Molecules, Part I (1913), pp. 8–9, Niels Bohr interprets existing hydrogen discharge and astronomical spectra. Electrical discharge in a vacuum tube removes electrons; recombination supplies spectral lines. This is a theoretical interpretation, without a reported spectrograph of his own.[ref]
An actual optical obstacle appears in Theodore Lyman's measurements: hydrogen discharge light entered an evacuated spectrograph directly through a slit, avoiding a transmitting window. A concave reflection diffraction grating dispersed the light onto photographic film. Pumping preserved the vacuum; a second slit supplied a known spectral displacement for wavelength calibration. Gas contamination and vacuum leaks limited the measurement. This apparatus resolved ultraviolet spectral lines; it did not image orbits.[ref]
For a separate original calibration exercise, suppose an idealized spectrograph returns synthetic vacuum line positions xn​=λn→2​+b for n=3,4,5,6, with chosen additive offset b=0.200nm. Assume its dispersion scale is already known and only this offset is uncertain. Compare the finite-mass prediction with the fixed-nucleus prediction λn(∞)​=(μ/me​)λn→2​. Calibrate each model using only the 3→2 line: b=x3​−λ3model​. Then hold that offset fixed and test the other lines with residuals
dn​=xn​−b−λnmodel​.
(20)
For the finite-mass model every dn​=0. The fixed-nucleus model has b=0.55733nm and residuals d4​=−0.09264nm, d5​=−0.12100nm, d6​=−0.13400nm. Algebraically dn​=(1−μ/me​)(λn​−λ3​): one additive calibration cannot absorb a multiplicative change of the wavelengths. Allowing an unknown multiplicative dispersion factor as well would make the two models degenerate in this exercise, so independent scale calibration matters.

Coulomb radial origin condition (u=rR,u(0)=0,R(r)∼rℓ)

Words: 114
Radial Schrodinger equation for the hydrogen atom OurBigBook.com
For the usual three-dimensional Coulomb potential Hamiltonian operator, a separated radial wavefunction R(r) uses the reduced function u=rR, whose radial norm has measure dr. The regular physical operator domain imposes u(0)=0. Near the origin the leading radial equation gives the indicial equation c(c−1)−ℓ(ℓ+1)=0 for u∼rc, with roots c=ℓ+1 and c=−ℓ.
The regular root gives R∼rℓ. The other root gives R∼r−ℓ−1, and its radial probability integral ∫0ε​r2∣R∣2dr∼∫0ε​r−2ℓdr diverges for ℓ≥1. At ℓ=0, R∼1/r is locally square-integrable in three dimensions, but violates u(0)=0 and has divergent kinetic energy integral ∫0ε​r2∣R′∣2dr∼∫0ε​r−2dr. Thus local wavefunction normalization alone is insufficient to select the physical branch in this exceptional case; the standard Coulomb energy domain supplies the missing condition.

Formal symmetry and these identities do not establish a self-adjoint momentum observable on the half-line; domains and origin conditions must be specified when taking adjoints or defining products.

Stark effect

Words: 2k Articles: 12
Mathematical physics OurBigBook.com
An electric field shifts and can split the energy eigenvalues of an atom. This is the Stark effect; its hydrogen atom ground-state case is quadratic in a weak field.
The observable in Stark effect spectroscopy is a change in a spectral line, rather than a direct reading of an individual energy eigenvalue. If an upper energy eigenstate u emits a photon into a lower energy eigenstate l, the Planck constant h relates its frequency to the difference:
hν(E)=Eu​(E)−El​(E),hΔν=ΔEu​−ΔEl​.
(38)
Here E denotes the applied electric field component along a chosen axis. Both levels can move, and electric-dipole selection rules for hydrogen decide which pairs produce observable spectral lines. This makes Stark effect spectroscopy a probe of energy eigenstates and their electric dipole moments: the slope −∂E/∂E is the corresponding dipole component by the Hellmann–Feynman theorem. The comparison with Zeeman splitting is useful: there an applied magnetic field supplies the perturbation.

Stark effect OurBigBook.com
The energy shift produced by an oscillating electric field, often called a light shift. For a far-detuned two-level drive with coupling ℏΩ/2 and Δ=ωL​−ωeg​, the ground-state shift is approximately ℏ∣Ω∣2/(4Δ). Multilevel atoms can have polarization-dependent differential shifts.

Rotational Stark effect

Stark canal-ray experiment

Words: 362
Stark effect OurBigBook.com
In 1913 Johannes Stark reported that an applied electric field resolved the hydrogen Hβ​ and Hγ​ spectral lines into five components at his instrument's spectral resolving power, viewed perpendicular to the electric field. Three inner components had polarization of an electromagnetic wave perpendicular to the electric field; two outer components had it parallel.[ref]
In his lecture of 3 June 1920 for the 1919 prize, Johannes Stark describes canal rays emerging through a perforated cathode into the electric field between it and a supplementary electrode. A spectrograph recorded the emitted light. His earlier Doppler effect comparison used a collimator perpendicular to the beam and then along approaching rays. Later beam/electric field reversal changed component intensities.[ref]
The historical account distinguishes observation perpendicular to the electric field, with five resolved components, from observation parallel to it, with three. These are viewing directions, distinct from the direction of the polarization of an electromagnetic wave.[ref]
The experimental distinctions matter. Changing the viewing direction tests a Doppler effect contribution; changing the applied electric field tests the Stark effect; analyzing polarization of an electromagnetic wave separates components that may overlap in an unpolarized record. A comparison with the unperturbed spectral line fixes the origin of a displacement. These are different controls, and the earlier Doppler effect comparison should not be described as a field-off control of the later discovery. A spectrograph's finite spectral resolving power can merge several components into one. In particular, a count of visible spectral lines does not by itself count all energy eigenstates.
For a modern idealization of the gap, an electric potential difference ΔV over separation d gives ∣E∣≃∣ΔV∣/d only if edge effects and the charge density in the gas are negligible. This is a calibration model, not a historical value assigned to Stark's apparatus. Similarly, a canal ray beam need not be a pure beam of neutral excited hydrogen atoms; the quantum mechanics model below isolates one neutral hydrogen atom from the source's preparation and collision processes.

Kepler's laws of planetary motion

Words: 954 Articles: 4
Mathematical physics OurBigBook.com
Kepler's laws describe three connected features of an elliptic orbit: its shape, how fast it is traversed, and how its size determines its orbital period. Kepler's first law gives an ellipse with the attracting centre at one focus of a conic; Kepler's second law gives equal swept areas in equal times; Kepler's third law relates the squared orbital period to the cubed semi-major axis. Together they turn a drawing of a Kepler orbit into a prediction of where the bodies will be and when they will return. [ref]
Here the mathematical model is an isolated two-body problem in Newtonian gravity, with point masses M,m>0 and a bound, noncolliding elliptic orbit. Let r=rm​−rM​ be the relative displacement, r=∣r∣ the separation, and μ=G(M+m) the gravitational parameter, where G is the gravitational constant. Newton's law of universal gravitation then gives
r¨=−r3μ​r.
(50)
The relative Kepler orbit has semi-major axis a and orbital eccentricity 0≤e<1. Both bodies move around their shared astronomical barycenter, the system's centre of mass. In its rest frame their displacements are rm​=Mr/(M+m) and rM​=−mr/(M+m). Their individual semi-major axes therefore add to a; the relative ellipse's attracting focus of a conic represents zero separation, rather than a body fixed in space.
One example will connect all three laws. After nondimensionalization, choose a=1, e=0.6 and μ=1. The semi-minor axis is b=a1−e2​=0.8, while the periapsis distance and apoapsis distance are
rp​=a(1−e)=0.4,ra​=a(1+e)=1.6.
(51)
Thus a=(0.4+1.6)/2=1 measures the ellipse's size even though the separation changes fourfold. The specific angular momentum will be 0.8, the two endpoint speeds 2 and 0.5, and the orbital period 2π. These are values in the chosen scaled units, not measurements of a particular planet.
Johannes Kepler published Kepler's first law and Kepler's second law in Astronomia Nova in 1609 and Kepler's third law in Harmonices Mundi in 1619. These publication dates are documented by [ref]. Their appeal is that three short statements organize both geometry and timing; Newtonian gravity supplies a common dynamical explanation.

Kepler's third law (T2=4π2a3/[G(M+m)])

Words: 302 Articles: 1
Kepler's laws of planetary motion OurBigBook.com
For an isolated two-body problem in Newtonian gravity, the relative elliptic orbit's orbital period T obeys
T2=G(M+m)4π2a3​=μ4π2a3​.
(52)
Here a is the relative semi-major axis, and M+m is the sum of the two masses. The separation r varies during an elliptic orbit, so replacing a by r works only for a circular orbit, where r=a. Likewise, either body's individual semi-major axis about the centre of mass must first be converted to the relative one. When m is negligible compared with M, the denominator can be approximated by GM.
For fixed gravitational parameter, the orbital period depends on the semi-major axis and is independent of orbital eccentricity. Our a=1, μ=1 example gives T=2π both for e=0.6 and for a circular orbit with e=0. The eccentric body's rapidly changing speed compensates for its different path. A compact way to see the cancellation uses Kepler's second law: divide the ellipse's area πab by its areal velocity h/2. With b=a1−e2​ and specific angular momentum h=μa(1−e2)​, the result is 2πa3/μ​.
Compare two separate Kepler orbits with the same gravitational parameter, a1​=1 and a2​=4:
T1​T2​​=(a1​a2​​)3/2=43/2=8.
(53)
With μ=1, their orbital periods are 2π and 16π; measured in units of T1​, these are 1 and 8. Quadrupling the size therefore takes eight times as long to complete a circuit. This power law makes comparisons possible without first choosing physical units.
The same relation can be inverted to weigh a system: M+m=4π2a3/(GT2). An observed relative semi-major axis and orbital period determine the total mass, while additional information is needed to separate the two masses. This is useful for binary stars, as discussed in NASA, Orbits and Kepler's Laws: measuring masses. Geometry and a clock together become a weighing instrument.

Kepler's second law (dA/dt=h/2)

Words: 308
Kepler's laws of planetary motion OurBigBook.com
The relative displacement of a Kepler orbit sweeps equal areas about the attracting focus of a conic in equal times. A short interval near periapsis covers a wide angle at small separation; the same interval near apoapsis covers a narrow angle at large separation. The swept areas are equal even though the travelled distances are different. In particular, the sectors have curved ellipse boundaries: triangles formed by joining their endpoints only approximate the swept areas for short intervals.
Let h=∣r×r˙∣ be the relative specific angular momentum. The areal velocity is
dtdA​=21​∣r×r˙∣=2h​.
(55)
A central force exerts zero torque about its centre, so conservation of angular momentum makes this rate constant. This explanation also applies to other central forces; the ellipse shape specifically comes from Newtonian gravity.
In the a=1, e=0.6, μ=1 example, specific angular momentum is h=μa(1−e2)​=0.64​=0.8, giving areal velocity 0.4. At periapsis and apoapsis, the velocity is perpendicular to the relative displacement, so h=rv. The endpoint speeds are consequently
vp​=0.40.8​=2,va​=1.60.8​=0.5.
(56)
The fourfold speed difference is consistent with the fourfold separation difference. Away from these endpoints, h/r gives only the transverse component of velocity; the full speed follows from the vis-viva equation.
To actually place equal-time markers, use Kepler's equation. Write mean anomaly as M=nt, with t=0 at periapsis and mean motion n=μ/a3​=1. The different symbol M avoids confusing this angle with the mass M. Solve for eccentric anomaly E in radians, then compute the relative position:
M=E−esinE,x=a(cosE−e),y=bsinE.
(57)
This timing procedure is explained in NASA educational archive, How Orbital Motion is Calculated.
For the first interval 0≤t≤π/6, the final eccentric anomaly is E≈1.041495. For the equal interval π≤t≤7π/6 starting at apoapsis, it ends at E≈3.471065. Both swept areas are ΔA=(h/2)Δt=0.4π/6=π/15≈0.209440, one twelfth of the entire ellipse's area 0.8π. The diagram computes its markers from Kepler's equation, making visible how uniform time steps become uneven spatial steps.

Two-patch vector potential for a radial monopole (A±​=rsinθ±1−cosθ​eϕ​,∇×A±​=er​/r2)

Magnetic monopole OurBigBook.com
The radial vector field B=er​/r2 on punctured three-dimensional Euclidean space has flux 4π through every centered sphere. It has no vector potential smooth on an entire enclosing sphere: the Stokes theorem on a closed surface would force zero flux. Two overlapping patches suffice. In spherical coordinates take A+​=(1−cosθ)eϕ​/(rsinθ), regular away from the negative z axis, and A−​=−(1+cosθ)eϕ​/(rsinθ), regular away from the positive z axis. Their curls both equal B.
The Cartesian forms A+​=(−y,x,0)/[r(r+z)] and A−​=(y,−x,0)/[r(r−z)] show that the first is smooth at the north pole and the second at the south pole. On the overlap their difference is A+​−A−​=2∇ϕ, where the azimuth ϕ is defined locally. Its multivaluedness around the axis explains the circulation difference 4π. Splitting the sphere along a latitude, applying the Stokes theorem with A+​ on the north and A−​ on the south, and using their opposite boundary orientations recovers the total flux. A coordinate singularity in the tangential spherical basis does not by itself make a vanishing smooth vector field singular at a pole.

Other reference frames assign different angular velocities and relative velocities, and hence different Coriolis forces to the same motion.
The cross product makes the Coriolis force perpendicular to both Ω and vrot​, with magnitude 2mΩ∣vrot​∣sinα, where α is the angle between them. The appeal of this description is practical: axes attached to the Earth or a turning apparatus can be kept fixed on the page, provided Newton's second law includes the extra terms. A free particle in rotating coordinates shows exactly how a straight laboratory trajectory can become curved, while Coriolis acceleration in local Earth coordinates gives a useful terrestrial scale. The rotating-table demonstration of Coriolis deflection makes the two viewpoints visible in one experiment.

Schrödinger equation (iℏ∂t​ψ=Hψ)

Words: 2k Articles: 17
Mathematical physics OurBigBook.com
The Schrödinger equation governs the evolution of a quantum state between instances of measurement in quantum mechanics. For a particle of mass m>0 moving in a prescribed real potential energy V(r,t), its position wavefunction satisfies
iℏ∂t∂ψ​=H(t)ψ,H(t)=−2mℏ2​∇2+V(r,t),ℏ=2πh​.
(78)
Here h is the Planck constant, ∇2 is the Laplace operator, and the Hamiltonian operator combines kinetic energy with potential energy. Specify an initial wavefunction, an operator domain and any boundary conditions: the differential expression alone does not completely specify a physical model. The Born rule then turns the evolving probability amplitude into position probabilities through ρ=∣ψ∣2 and integration over a region.
This scalar Schrödinger operator describes nonrelativistic quantum mechanics, with relevant momenta much smaller than mc, where c is the speed of light. It omits the constant rest energy mc2, assumes fixed particle number, and suppresses active spin dynamics and coupling to a magnetic vector potential. A free electron with a fixed, uncoupled spin state can still use this scalar model; the Pauli equation supplies the additional spin components and magnetic coupling when needed. A prescribed real V describes a closed evolution model or an approximation in which the source of that potential energy is treated as external. Dissipation, particle creation and a general measurement in quantum mechanics need further modelling.
For a time-independent self-adjoint Hamiltonian operator, the spectral theorem defines unitary time evolution by
ψ(t)=e−iHt/ℏψ(0),∥ψ(t)∥2=∥ψ(0)∥2.
(79)
Initial states in the operator domain satisfy the differential equation in the Hilbert space sense; the unitary operator also evolves all other states in that Hilbert space. Time-dependent Hamiltonian operators need suitable regularity and domain hypotheses; their evolution is not generally the exponential of −itH(t)/ℏ.
The local reason for conservation is especially tangible. Multiply the Schrödinger equation by the complex conjugate ψ∗, subtract its conjugate multiplied by ψ, and use the fact that the real potential energy terms cancel. For smooth wavefunctions this gives the probability continuity equation
∂t​ρ+∇⋅j=0,j=mℏ​Im(ψ∗∇ψ).
(80)
The divergence theorem identifies the change in probability inside a region with minus the outward probability current. Decay at infinity, or appropriate probability-conserving boundary conditions, preserves wavefunction normalization. Conservation of total probability does not require a stationary probability density.
Its usefulness comes from being a linear partial differential equation: quantum superpositions of solutions are solutions, while different quantum phases can produce interference. For a fixed Hamiltonian operator, the time-independent Schrödinger equation finds the energy eigenstates; each then acquires just its own time-dependent quantum phase. One eigenvalue problem therefore organizes both allowed energies and the evolution of arbitrary quantum superpositions, with a continuous spectrum included when required. This is the attractive bridge between a spatial wave problem and a clock: energy differences determine the rate at which relative quantum phases change. It makes atomic spectral lines, quantum tunnelling and quantum scattering calculable from a specified model.
For an explicit example without confinement, take a free particle on the whole line, V=0, initially in a Gaussian wave packet with position standard deviation σ0​ and mean momentum ℏk0​:

Unlike a single plane wave, this wavefunction satisfies wavefunction normalization. A Fourier transform writes it as a quantum superposition of plane waves. Their dispersion relation is ω(k)=ℏk2/(2m), so each Fourier component gains the factor e−iℏk2t/(2m). Completing the square in the resulting Gaussian integral gives
ψ(x,t)=(2πσ02​)1/41+iτ​1​exp[−4σ02​(1+iτ)(x−v0​t)2​+ik0​x−2miℏk02​t​],
(82)
with the square root chosen continuously from t=0. Its position probability density and standard deviation are
ρ(x,t)=2π​σt​exp[−(x−v0​t)2/(2σt2​)]​,σt​=σ0​1+τ2​.
(83)
The centre moves with the group velocity ω′(k0​)=v0​ and the wave packet spreads because different wavenumbers have different group velocities. This is unitary wave dispersion, without a random force or loss of probability. Independently, the initial momentum standard deviation is Δp=ℏ/(2σ0​) and the initial position-momentum covariance vanishes. Free evolution gives x(t)=x(0)+p(0)t/m in the Heisenberg picture, hence

This independently checks the spreading law. The Gaussian integral of ρ is one at every time; the decreasing peak is exactly offset by increasing width.

The complex width also explains where the probability goes. Write ψ=ρ​eiθ, where θ is the dimensionless quantum phase. Differentiating the exact solution gives

The probability within a moving interval of half-width σ0​ falls from about 0.6827 initially to 0.5205 at ts​, exactly because of this outward probability current.
Historically, the 1926 Quantisierung als Eigenwertproblem (Erste Mitteilung) by Erwin Schrödinger began with the stationary hydrogen atom problem. It distinguishes discrete negative energies from a positive continuous spectrum; it is not yet the general evolution equation displayed above.[ref] The opening of quantum mechanics discusses its original vibrating-string analogy.
In the 12 December 1933 lecture The fundamental idea of wave mechanics by Erwin Schrödinger, Erwin Schrödinger explains the move from independent rays to waves through diffraction, then applies that analogy to atomic physics. His closing pages explicitly acknowledge the difficulty of reconciling wave language with observed particle tracks. This retrospective physical argument motivates the model; it does not derive the modern Born rule from classical mechanics.[ref]
The dates separate proposal from measurement: the de Broglie wavelength belongs to the 1924 thesis, the Schrödinger equation to 1926, and the Davisson–Germer experiment's electron diffraction beams to 1927.[ref] That linked experiment describes the prepared nickel crystal, evacuated electron gun, angular collector scans, retarding-potential selection and heating controls. Its measured collector electric current tests wave-dependent scattering probabilities; it neither measures a wavefunction directly nor establishes this equation uniquely.

The geostrophic wind is the horizontal flow for which the pressure gradient force balances the Coriolis force. It runs along atmospheric isobars and has speed proportional to their pressure gradient, at fixed density and nonzero Coriolis parameter. Curvature, friction and small spatial scales can invalidate that approximation.

Geostrophic wind OurBigBook.com
A steady horizontal parcel with drag acceleration −ru obeys 0=−∇h​p/ρ−fz^×u−ru. Inverting the horizontal rotation-plus-drag matrix gives the title. For r>0, the velocity has a component toward lower pressure and a component along atmospheric isobars. For px​=0, f>0, py​>0, both u,v are negative. The cross-isobar angle is arctan(r/f), and the speed is smaller than the corresponding frictionless wind. A vertically resolved turbulent stress is not generally equivalent to one constant r.

Dot the steady linear-drag momentum equation with the velocity. The Coriolis force does no work, so pressure-gradient work balances frictional dissipation. In a strictly geostrophic flow the wind is along isobars and pressure work vanishes. Cross-isobar motion supplies the positive pressure work needed to maintain a dissipative equilibrium.

With x eastward and y northward, a purely meridional pressure gradient gives the velocity in the title. For f>0, pressure increasing northward gives westward wind, leaving lower pressure to the wind's left. Reversing the pressure gradient reverses the velocity. At a fixed gradient and density the speed scales as 1/∣sinϕ∣; the formal equatorial divergence signals breakdown of geostrophic balance, rather than a real infinite wind.

Entropy condition (∂t​η(u)+∂x​Q(u)≤0)

Words: 89
Conservation law OurBigBook.com
For a scalar conservation law ut​+q(u)x​=0, an entropy condition restricts its weak solutions to physically admissible ones. For every convex entropy function η, define an entropy flux by Q′=η′q′. The displayed inequality is imposed in the distributional sense. Positive diffusion explains this choice: for ut​+q(u)x​=ϵ[D(u)ux​]x​ with D>0, the entropy balance is η(u)t​+Q(u)x​=ϵ[η′(u)D(u)ux​]x​−ϵη′′(u)D(u)ux2​. The last term is nonpositive, and an appropriate vanishing-diffusion limit yields the entropy inequality. For a strictly concave flux and a single shock, this selects states with incoming characteristics, rather than a discontinuity whose characteristics spread outward.

Standing wave

Words: 1k Articles: 7
Mathematical physics OurBigBook.com
A standing wave results from the superposition principle applied to equal-frequency, equal-amplitude waves travelling in opposite directions. Its spatial nodes of a standing wave remain fixed while its displacement oscillates in time.
For a pure standing wave, the two travelling waves also have equal amplitudes: their interference leaves a fixed mode shape, rather than a profile moving along the string. Choose the position origin and time origin so that their transverse displacements are
y+​(x,t)=asin(kx−ωt),y−​(x,t)=asin(kx+ωt).
(103)
Here a>0 is each constituent's amplitude, k=2π/λ is the wavenumber, λ is the wavelength, and ω=2πf is the angular frequency corresponding to frequency f. Their wave speed is c=ω/k. The superposition principle and the sine addition formula give
y=y+​+y−​=2asin(kx)cos(ωt).
(104)
The spatial factor stays put; the temporal factor changes its size and sign. Other constant wave phases shift the position or time origin. Unequal constituent amplitudes generally leave moving displacement at the would-be nodes of a standing wave, rather than this exact factorization.[ref]
For an original ideal-string example, set L=1m, c=20ms−1, and choose the third normal mode. Then k=3πm−1, ω=60πs−1, and f=30Hz by fixed-end standing wave frequencies. With each constituent amplitude a=5mm,
y(x,t)=0.010msin(1m3πx​)cos(1s60πt​).
(105)
Its nodes of a standing wave are at x=0,1/3,2/3,1m and its antinodes at x=1/6,1/2,5/6m. These are constructed model parameters, not experimental readings.
At t=1/120s, every point has zero displacement, but most have nonzero transverse velocity: the string is crossing its straight configuration. The black dots alone mark permanent nodes of a standing wave. At an antinode the greatest transverse speed is 2aω=0.6πms−1, much smaller than the chosen 20ms−1 wave speed. One is motion of string material; the other is propagation of the constituent profiles.
The beauty of a standing wave is that motion reveals geometry: fixed nodes of a standing wave turn a moving disturbance into a spatial ruler. Their separation measures wavelength, and boundary conditions turn the continuous choice of wavenumber into a discrete set of normal modes. This is useful both for interpreting string vibrations and for understanding how a bounded wave equation selects its eigenfrequencies.

Standing-and-travelling decomposition of a reflected string wave

Words: 57
Standing wave OurBigBook.com
For real negative displacement reflection amplitude r=−a, with 0<a<1, use
A[cos(kx−ωt)−acos(kx+ωt)]=(1−a)Acos(kx−ωt)+2aAsinkxsinωt.
(106)
This separates a travelling field and a standing field algebraically. Their individual powers cannot be treated as independent incident-power fractions because the two fields interfere. Reflected and transmitted power should instead be calculated from travelling-wave amplitudes with the appropriate characteristic impedance factors.

Pinned-square surface displacement mode (knm​=πn2+m2​/L)

Words: 66
Standing wave OurBigBook.com
A surface displacement constrained to vanish on all four sides of an ideal square has sine factors sin(nπx/L)sin(mπy/L), with n,m≥1. The fundamental therefore has wavenumber 2​π/L. This differs from the impermeable-wall condition in a closed tank, which permits cosine modes with a zero index. For an elastic plate a simply supported edge also supplies its bending boundary condition; clamping imposes a different problem.

Two-mode string recurrence (ω1​t,ω2​t∈2πZ)

Words: 68
Standing wave OurBigBook.com
For two distinct sine normal modes with nonzero amplitudes and initial cosine phases zero, linear independence of their spatial profiles means the initial shape returns exactly only when both time factors equal one. A rational frequency ratio ω2​/ω1​=p/q in lowest terms gives first positive recurrence 2πq/ω1​. An irrational ratio gives no exact positive recurrence, although arbitrarily close two-mode returns exist. These statements refer to the complete spatial profile, not a displacement at one observation point.

Standing wave node spacing (Δx=λ/2)

Words: 136
Standing wave OurBigBook.com
A node of a standing wave must have y(x,t)=0 for every time, not merely at one snapshot. For y=2asin(kx)cos(ωt), with a,k,ω>0, set t=0 to see that this requires sin(kx)=0. Thus
xj​=kjπ​=2jλ​,xj+1​−xj​=2λ​,j∈Z.
(107)
An antinode instead maximizes the oscillation amplitude 2a∣sin(kx)∣ and lies halfway between successive nodes of a standing wave, at x=(2j+1)λ/4. Neighbouring antinodes are also separated by λ/2; the distance from a node of a standing wave to its nearest antinode is λ/4. These distances refer to the string's longitudinal coordinate, not its curved arc length.
Within one interval between nodes of a standing wave, all moving points have the same oscillation phase. Adjacent intervals have opposite signs of sin(kx), so their phase difference is π: one loop rises while the next falls. The oscillation phase at an exact node of a standing wave is undefined because its amplitude is zero. A ruler measures the spacing of the fixed pattern; it does not track a moving wave crest.

Fixed-end standing wave frequencies (kn​=nπ/L,fn​=nc/(2L))

Words: 184
Standing wave OurBigBook.com
For the ideal uniform wave equation on a string, the wave speed is c=τ/μ​, where τ is constant tension and μ is linear mass density. Assume small transverse slopes, negligible bending stiffness and no damping. Fix both ends at zero displacement, giving the homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions y(0,t)=y(L,t)=0. Our standing wave already satisfies the first. For a nonzero amplitude, the second requires sin(kL)=0, hence
kn​=Lnπ​,λn​=n2L​,ωn​=ckn​,fn​=2πωn​​=2Lnc​,n=1,2,3,….
(108)
The value n=0 gives zero displacement in this sine family, not a vibrating normal mode. Each positive n fits n half-wavelengths into the string: it has n antinodes, n−1 interior nodes of a standing wave, and two endpoint nodes of a standing wave. For L=1m and c=20ms−1, fn​=10nHz; the third normal mode has f3​=30Hz and wavelength 2/3m.
The equally spaced eigenfrequencies follow from this string's uniform wave speed and fixed-end boundary conditions. They are not a universal spectrum for every vibrating object. Changing an endpoint constraint changes the allowed mode shapes; changing tension changes wave speed. At fixed L and μ, quadrupling τ doubles every fn​. The more general construction of arbitrary initial motion belongs to normal mode and wave equation on a string.

Standing wave phase and energy (⟨P⟩t​=0)

Words: 201
Standing wave OurBigBook.com
A stationary mode shape does not imply absence of energy. Write A=2a and y=Asin(kx)cos(ωt). For the ideal wave equation on a string, the kinetic energy and elastic potential energy per unit reference length add to
e=2μ​yt2​+2τ​yx2​,P=−τyx​yt​.
(109)
Here P is signed power crossing a position on the string, positive to the right; e is an energy density per length, not per volume. Differentiation and μytt​=τyxx​ give the local conservation of energy identity ∂t​e+∂x​P=0. Substitution into P gives
P(x,t)=τA2kωsin(kx)cos(kx)sin(ωt)cos(ωt).
(110)
It can be nonzero away from a node of a standing wave or an antinode, but its time average over an oscillation period is zero. Energy flows locally back and forth even though this pure standing wave transports no net energy across a section over a complete cycle. At a node of a standing wave, yt​=0, so kinetic energy density is zero, but yx​ need not vanish: elastic potential energy density can be positive there.
For a fixed-end normal mode, integration over 0≤x≤L gives
K(t)=4μA2ω2L​sin2(ωt),U(t)=4τA2k2L​cos2(ωt),E=K+U=4μA2ω2L​.
(111)
The last equality uses τk2=μω2. At a straight-string snapshot, U=0 while K=E; at an extreme snapshot, K=0 while U=E. This is normal-mode energy exchange. A driven real string with damping requires continuing input power to replace lost energy, so a visually stationary pattern does not establish zero average supplied power.

Driven string standing wave experiment

Words: 218
Standing wave OurBigBook.com
The University of California, Santa Barbara's cord demonstration uses a function generator and mechanical driver loosely attached near a clamped cord end. The other end passes over a pulley to a mass hanger, setting tension. Its photograph shows operation with a strobe; the page reports measured and calculated lowest-mode frequencies. Varying drive frequency at fixed loading selects higher normal modes. This clamp arrangement differs from a string tied directly to a moving driver.[ref]
A controlled frequency scan holds the cord, endpoint separation and hanging load fixed, then varies frequency slowly to locate large steady amplitudes. Read stationary nodes of a standing wave and count loops; compare the inferred λ=2L/n with c=fλ. As additional checks, compare small drive settings, repeat the scan in reverse, and change only the hanging load to test the predicted square-root tension dependence. These checks test the ideal model rather than adding measurements to the demonstration.
An elastic cord's stretched linear mass density can differ from its relaxed value; the published calculation uses the relaxed value. A strobe can freeze motion at misleading settings, so identify nodes of a standing wave across several snapshots. A moving attachment need not be an exact node of a standing wave. These limits qualify any comparison with ideal fixed-end eigenfrequencies.[ref]
